notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Nahum 3, drawn from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Nahum 3 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Structure of the Chapter

Commentators consistently divide the chapter into three or four sections. David Guzik (Enduring Word) traces three reasons Nineveh is ripe for judgment: (1) her own sinful character (vv. 1–7), (2) the example of Thebes (vv. 8–11), and (3) the weakness of her leadership and defences (vv. 12–19). The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics similarly sees vv. 1–7 as the guilt, vv. 8–13 as the sign of No-Amon, and vv. 14–19 as the fall. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/nahum/3.htm

---

### v. 1 — "Woe to the city of blood, full of lies, full of plunder, never without prey."

- **Gill** notes that "bloody city" (lit. "city of bloods") refers to Nineveh's murders, unjust judicial killings, and constant warfare against neighbouring nations to enlarge its wealth. "Lies and robbery" refer to the deceit and rapine found in both palace and marketplace. "The prey departeth not" means Nineveh never ceased making a prey of others. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nahum-3.html

- **Ellicott** translates: "O bloody city! She is altogether deceit, filled with crime: she ceases not from plunder." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **JFB** explains: "city of blood—namely, shed by Nineveh; just so now her own blood is to be shed." It adds that the verb for "departeth not" is transitive: "she (Nineveh) does not make the prey depart"—she never stops plundering. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Guzik (Enduring Word)** adds that Assyrian rulers not only committed cruelty but boasted of it on monuments (flaying skin, building pillars of human bodies), showing a pride that made them ripe for humbling. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

- **Pulpit Homiletics** calls this "a mournful revelation of national guilt": unrighteous war, cunning craftiness ("full of lies"), and continuous spoliation—all despite the earlier repentance under Jonah. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/nahum/3.htm

---

### v. 2 — "The crack of the whip, the rumble of the wheel, galloping horse and bounding chariot!"

- **Ellicott** translates: "Hark to the whip, and hark to the rattling of the wheel, and the horse galloping, and the chariot bounding." He says this describes the entry of the victorious besiegers. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **Gill** explains these are the sounds of the invading army approaching Nineveh, "striking terror into them." The whip urges on the horses, the wheels rattle on stones, the horses prance at full gallop, and the chariots seem to "leap and dance" from the speed. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nahum-3.html

- **JFB** says "the reader is transported into the midst of the fight" (cf. Jeremiah 47:3). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Guzik** notes that Nahum saw a busy city "full of the noise of a whip … of rattling wheels, of galloping horses, of clattering chariots," yet busy with violence and deception, not honest labour. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

---

### v. 3 — "Charging horseman, flashing sword, shining spear; heaps of slain, mounds of corpses, dead bodies without end—they stumble over their dead—"

- **JFB** renders the Hebrew: "the glitter of the sword and the flash of the spear!" and explains the horseman is distinct from the horses in the chariots of v. 2. "They stumble upon their corpses"—the Medo-Babylonian enemy stumble upon the Assyrian corpses. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Ellicott** translates: "There is the rearing horseman and the flaming sword, and the glittering lance, and a multitude of wounded, and a mass of corpses…" — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **Guzik** notes this was "literally fulfilled." He cites Diodorus Siculus: "So great was the multitude of the slain that the flowing stream, mingled with their blood, changed its color for a considerable distance." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

---

### v. 4 — "because of the many harlotries of the harlot, the seductive mistress of sorcery, who betrays nations by her prostitution and clans by her witchcraft."

- **Ellicott** provides the most detailed historical background: In the idolatry and superstition of Nineveh the prophet finds the cause of destruction. The Babylonian worship of Beltis/Mylitta involved a system of female prostitution deemed "most shameful" even by the heathen historian Herodotus. The same deity was worshipped in Assyria. Professor Rawlinson suggests the prophet alludes to this practice. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **JFB** notes that since Assyria was not a worshipper of the true God, "whoredoms" here cannot mean apostasy from true religion (as with Israel). Rather, it refers to "harlot-like artifices, whereby she allured neighbouring states so as to subject them to herself"—using plausible professions and the lure of commerce. "Witchcrafts" alludes to love incantations used by harlots, corresponding to Assyria's subtle machinations. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Gill** provides extensive detail on both literal and spiritual harlotry: the legend of Semiramis (a former harlot), Sardanapalus's effeminacy, and the compulsory prostitution of Assyrian women in the temple of Venus/Mylitta. He also notes that idolatry is "frequently expressed by whoredom and adultery" in Scripture, and that Nineveh is a type of "the whore of Rome" (Revelation 17:1). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nahum-3.html

- **Guzik** points out that Nineveh not only indulged in sin itself but "sells the nations through her harlotries"—she led others into violence, deception, and idolatry. He cites Maier: "Thousands of tablets uncovered in the Mesopotamian valley show abysmal superstition. Hundreds of sorcery incantations have been brought to light." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

- **Precept Austin** notes that the chief deity of Nineveh was Ishtar, "goddess of sexual passion, fertility, and war," which explains why Nahum used the harlotry metaphor. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/nahum-devotionals-and-sermon-illustrations

---

### v. 5 — "Behold, I am against you,' declares the LORD of Hosts. 'I will lift your skirts over your face. I will show your nakedness to the nations and your shame to the kingdoms.'"

- **Guzik** notes this phrase repeats Nahum 2:13; the first emphasis was military defeat, now it is the humbling of the city. He ties it to 1 Peter 5:5: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

- **JFB** explains: "I will treat thee not as a matron, but as a harlot, whose shame is exposed, her gaudy finery being lifted up off her (Isaiah 47:2-3). So Nineveh shall be stripped of all her glory and defenses on which she prides herself." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Gill**: "turn up the skirts of her garments over her head, and thereby discover what should be concealed, than which nothing is more disagreeable and abominable to modest persons; … she should be used in character as a harlot, or as women oftentimes are by rude soldiers, when a city is taken by them." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nahum-3.html

---

### v. 6 — "I will pelt you with filth and treat you with contempt; I will make a spectacle of you."

- **Guzik** explains that "abominable filth" translates the Hebrew *shiqquts*, often rendered "abomination"—God will take Nineveh's idols and "throw them back in their faces." The Hebrew word for "vile" (*nabel*) means "made weak, foolish, and contemptible." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

- **JFB**: treatment "as infamous harlots used to be treated," exposed to public ignominy as a warning (Ezekiel 28:17). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Gill** notes: "as dirt and dung, or any or everything that is abominable and filthy; and which is thrown at harlots publicly disgraced." The city would be "stripped of everything that was great and glorious." Kimchi interprets "gazingstock" as "dung." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nahum-3.html

---

### v. 7 — "Then all who see you will recoil from you and say, 'Nineveh is devastated; who will grieve for her?' Where can I find comforters for you?"

- **Ellicott**: Men flee from the stricken city lest they share her punishment, as in the destruction of Korah. "Nor is she an object of compassion whose cruelties have been as extensive as her empire." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **Guzik** cites Adam Clarke (writing before Nineveh's ruins were discovered in 1840): "Great as it was formerly, so little of it is remaining, that authors are not agreed even about its situation." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

- **Gill**: "there are none left in her to do it; and as for others, her neighbours, whom she has oppressed and cruelly used, these will laugh and rejoice, instead of lamenting." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nahum-3.html

- **Pulpit Homiletics**: This is "the entire absence of sympathy towards her in her reverses. … She should be thought of only as a beacon and a warning." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/nahum/3.htm

---

### v. 8 — "Are you better than Thebes, stationed by the Nile with water around her, whose rampart was the sea, whose wall was the water?"

- **Ellicott** gives the most detailed historical explanation: "No Amon" is Thebes, the capital of Upper Egypt, known to the Hebrews as "No Amon" (perhaps "house of the god Amon"). Assyria herself had reduced Thebes—either under Sargon (c. 716 BC), Esar-haddon (c. 670 BC), or Asshur-bani-pal (c. 665 BC). "To mere human reasoning the downfall of Thebes testified to the power of Assyria, its conqueror. But to the inspired vision of Nahum, the ruin of the one world-power is an earnest of the ruin of the other." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **JFB** notes the Nile is called a "sea" from its appearance in the annual flood (cf. Isaiah 19:5). Homer's Iliad mentions Thebes' hundred gates. Its ruins still describe a circuit of twenty-seven miles. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Gill** provides extensive discussion on whether No refers to Thebes, Alexandria, or Memphis, with detailed geographical and historical evidence for each. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nahum-3.html

- **Guzik**: "The Assyrians in Nineveh knew this well because it was their armies that destroyed Thebes. Nahum said to the Assyrians, 'Remember what you did to No Amon? The same is coming on you.'" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

---

### v. 9 — "Cush and Egypt were her boundless strength; Put and Libya were her allies."

- **JFB**: Cush (Ethiopia) was at this time mistress of Upper Egypt; Put (Phut) was probably west of Lower Egypt, conterminous with Libya Proper; Lubim were the Libyans whose capital was Cyrene. These were all auxiliaries of Thebes. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Ellicott**: If Nineveh relies on subordinate states, had not Thebes all the resources of Africa—Ethiopia in the south, the Egypts in the north, her Libyan allies in the north-west? — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

---

### v. 10 — "Yet she became an exile; she went into captivity. Her infants were dashed to pieces at the head of every street. They cast lots for her dignitaries, and all her nobles were bound in chains."

- **Ellicott**: Thebes' youth were carried off in slave-gangs; her infants dashed to pieces at the street-corner (cf. 2 Kings 8:12) as unprofitable to the captor; her senators reserved to grace a triumph and assigned to Assyrian generals by lot. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **JFB**: "notwithstanding all her might, she was overcome." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

---

### v. 11 — "You too will become drunk; you will go into hiding and seek refuge from the enemy."

- **JFB**: "Thou also shalt be drunken"—made to drink the cup of Yahweh's wrath (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). "Thou shalt be hid"—according to Hebrew idiom, "thou shalt so vanish out of sight as though thou hadst not been," referring to Nineveh's utter extinction so that her very site was for ages unknown. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Ellicott**: "Nineveh also shall be drunken with the cup of God's wrath (Habakkuk 2:16), yea, hid from recollection, so that men shall ask, 'Where is Nineveh?'" — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

---

### v. 12 — "All your fortresses are fig trees with the first ripe figs; when shaken, they fall into the mouth of the eater!"

- **Guzik**: "As easily as ripe fruit falls from a shaken tree, so would the strongholds of Nineveh fall before the judgment of God." He applies this to the "strongholds of sin and pride that we put great confidence in." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

- **JFB**: Expresses "the rapidity and ease of the capture of Nineveh" (cf. Isaiah 28:4; Revelation 6:13). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

---

### v. 13 — "Look at your troops—they are like your women! The gates of your land are wide open to your enemies; fire consumes their bars."

- **Ellicott**: "Thy people … are women" refers not to effeminate habits (though Nineveh was notoriously luxurious) but to "their panic-stricken condition at the time of the catastrophe. They are fearful as women (comp. Jeremiah 50:37; Jeremiah 51:30), because they find avenues laid open to the enemy." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **JFB**: "Thy people—thy soldiers … unable to fight for thee." The "gates of thy land" are the fortified passes or entrances to the region of Nineveh. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

---

### v. 14 — "Draw your water for the siege; strengthen your fortresses. Work the clay and tread the mortar; repair the brick kiln!"

- **Ellicott** calls this "scoffing advice": "In this desperate plight Nineveh is scoffingly advised to protract her resistance. … Let her lay in water and provision, and build new buttresses of brick. What shall it avail her?" He compares Nahum's irony to Isaiah's mockery of idol-makers (Isaiah 44:12ff). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **Guzik**: "Nahum practically mocked the people of Nineveh, cheering them on to do the best they could in light of the coming judgment. They could prepare as many provisions and people as they pleased, but it would all come to nothing against the judgment of God." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

- **JFB**: An "ironical exhortation to Nineveh to defend herself"—draw water, repair brick-kilns for new fortifications. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

---

### v. 15 — "There the fire will devour you; the sword will cut you down and consume you like a young locust. Make yourself many like the young locust; make yourself many like the swarming locust!"

- **Ellicott** notes the "diversion of metaphor" here: the sword, like the locust, shall devour Nineveh; then Nineveh herself is compared to a locust swarm—a "transition like St. Paul's 'going off at a word.'" Nineveh has been a locust-pest to the world. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **JFB**: "There"—in the very scene of your preparations. The fire, even as at the former destruction when Sardanapalus perished with his household in the conflagration of his palace, "the traces of which are still remaining." However many Nineveh's forces, "yet the foe shall consume thee as the 'licking locust' licks up all before it." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Guzik** notes archaeologists have "remarked on the large deposits of ash, which are evidence of a gigantic conflagration" (Boice). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

---

### v. 16 — "You have multiplied your merchants more than the stars of the sky. The young locust strips the land and flies away."

- **JFB**: Nineveh, by large canals, had easy access to Babylon and lay on the Tigris with access to the sea. Phoenician merchants carried its wares everywhere. He discusses three interpretations of the locust image: (1) the enemy spoils Nineveh's merchants and flees away; (2) Nineveh's merchants, having spoiled many regions, will themselves be scattered like locusts; (3) the locust "puts off" its wing-envelope and flies—so shall merchants be dispersed. He prefers the first view. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Ellicott** translates: "spreads itself out: swarms out to spoil." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

---

### v. 17 — "Your guards are like the swarming locust, and your scribes like clouds of locusts that settle on the walls on a cold day. When the sun rises, they fly away, and no one knows where."

- **Ellicott**: "Thy crowned" are the subordinate kings representing the Assyrian empire in her tributary provinces. "Captains" (*Taphs'rîm*) is an Assyrian term denoting high military office. He quotes Dr. Pusey: "The heathen conqueror rehearsed his victory, 'I came, I saw, I conquered.' The prophet goes further, as the issue of all human conquest, 'I disappeared.'" — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **JFB**: "Cold deprives the locust of the power of flight; so they alight in cold weather and at night, but when warmed by the sun soon 'flee away.' So shall the Assyrian multitudes suddenly disappear, not leaving a trace behind." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

---

### v. 18 — "O king of Assyria, your shepherds slumber; your officers sleep. Your people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them."

- **Ellicott**: "Shepherds" means chief officers (as in Micah 5:2). Their sheep are scattered "upon the mountains and none attempts to gather them"—echoing Micaiah's words to Ahab: "I saw all Israel scattered upon the hills as sheep that have not a shepherd" (1 Kings 22:17). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **JFB**: "Thy shepherds … slumber"—either "are carelessly secure" (Maurer) or "lie in death's sleep, having been slain" (Jerome). "Thy people is scattered" is the necessary consequence of leaders being laid low. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Guzik**: Each class of leaders (merchants, commanders, generals, shepherds, nobles) were numerous but "would all be ineffective and come to nothing in the day of judgment." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

---

### v. 19 — "There is no healing for your injury; your wound is severe. All who hear the news of you applaud your downfall, for who has not experienced your constant cruelty?"

- **JFB** gives the historical fulfillment: The Median attack on Nineveh came c. 633 BC, the final siege c. 625 BC. Saracus, the last king, collected his wives and treasures in his palace, set fire to it, and perished in the flames. "In strict fulfillment, Assyria never after rose to a national existence." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Ellicott**: "All that hear the 'bruit' or report of the fall of Nineveh clap their hands with joy (Psalm 47:1), for where has not her oppressive rule been felt?" The verse is addressed to the king (masculine singular in Hebrew) as the representative of the empire. Kleinert notes that the sculptures illustrate the cruelty: "rows of the impaled, the prisoners through whose lips rings were fastened, whose eyes were put out, who were flayed alive." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

- **Guzik** closes by citing Psalm 73 (Asaph's struggle with the prosperity of the wicked) and concludes: "We take comfort in knowing that the judgments of the LORD are faithful and true. We don't need to envy the unrighteous or seek vengeance against them ourselves." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

---

## Denominational Distinctives

### Reformed / Baptist

- **Gill (Reformed Baptist, 18th c.)** interprets the "whoredoms" of v. 4 as including a typological link to "the whore of Rome" (Revelation 17:1), a standard Protestant reading. He treats the literal and spiritual harlotry as intertwined. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nahum-3.html

- **JFB (Reformed/Evangelical)** specifically argues that since Assyria was not a worshipper of the true God, "whoredoms" cannot mean apostasy (as with Israel) but rather political and commercial seduction—a more restrained interpretation than Gill's. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nahum-3.html

- **Desiring God (John Piper, Reformed Baptist)** uses Nahum to teach about the storm of God's wrath, emphasizing God's holiness and the certainty of judgment on unrepentant sinners: "Nineveh took its stand against the awesome storm of God's wrath—and perished." Piper connects it to Matthew 25:41: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire." — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/how-to-read-a-thunderstorm

### Anglican

- **Ellicott (Anglican, 19th c.)** provides the richest historical-critical detail: precise identifications of Assyrian kings (Sargon, Esar-haddon, Asshur-bani-pal), Egyptian geography, and use of classical sources (Herodotus, Homer, Diodorus Siculus). He also provides more nuance on the dating of Nahum based on the Thebes reference. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/3.htm

### Pentecostal / Charismatic

- **Guzik (Enduring Word)** emphasizes the personal application of the text to the believer's life: strongholds of sin and pride are "ready to be shaken and fall to the ground." He draws the application that "we don't need to envy the wicked or seek our own vengeance." His commentary is more devotional and application-oriented than the older sources. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-3/

---

## What Could Not Be Found

I was unable to access the following within the available search/fetch limits:

- **Catholic readings** (newadvent.org, catholic.com) — for the Catholic understanding, e.g., whether the "whoredoms" are read as typological of the Church's enemies or with different emphasis
- **Orthodox readings** (oca.org) — for the Eastern patristic perspective
- **Lutheran sources** (lcms.org, 1517.org) — for the Law/Gospel hermeneutic on this judgment oracle
- **Methodist/Wesleyan sources** (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com) — for the holiness/personal sanctification reading
- **Modern scholarship** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) — for text-critical and archaeological notes
- **GTY / John MacArthur** — for the dispensational/premillennial perspective
- **Ligonier / Sproul** — for the specifically Reformed systematic reading
- **Spurgeon's full exposition** on Nahum 3 — only a brief mention of a sermon on v. 7 ("When Can We Find Comforters") was located

These would be worth searching for if a more comprehensive denominational comparison is needed.
